cls: Antiplatelet agent (P2Y12 ADP receptor inhibitor, thienopyridine)
pharm: Prodrug whose active metabolite irreversibly inhibits the platelet P2Y12 class of ADP receptors, blocking ADP-mediated platelet activation and aggregation for the platelet lifespan
quick: 60 mg oral loading dose, then 10 mg once daily (5 mg if <60 kg)
No human data; weigh bleeding risk and possible fetal risk
No human data; metabolites found in rat milk
No adjustment in mild-moderate; avoid in severe impairment
No specific interaction; excess raises bleeding/GI risk
Signs of bleeding; hemoglobin/hematocrit; platelets if TTP suspected
summary: Prasugrel is an oral P2Y12 platelet inhibitor used with aspirin to reduce thrombotic cardiovascular events (including stent thrombosis) in patients with acute coronary syndrome managed with PCI. It carries a BOXED WARNING for significant, sometimes fatal bleeding: it must not be used in active bleeding or in patients with a history of TIA or stroke, and is generally not recommended at age 75 or older except in selected high-risk patients.
indications: Acute coronary syndrome (unstable angina or NSTEMI) managed with PCI - to reduce thrombotic CV events including stent thrombosis
Acute coronary syndrome (STEMI) managed with primary or delayed PCI - to reduce thrombotic CV events including stent thrombosis

dosage.d: 60 mg oral loading dose, then 10 mg once daily
dosage.n: Co-administer daily aspirin 75-325 mg; may give with or without food

dosage.d: 60 mg load, then consider 5 mg once daily maintenance
dosage.n: Increased active-metabolite exposure and bleeding risk; 5 mg dose not prospectively studied
May be considered only in high-risk patients (diabetes or prior MI)

admin: Give a single 60 mg loading dose, then 10 mg once daily
May be taken with or without food
Do not break the tablet; dispense in original container
Do not start in patients likely to need urgent CABG
When possible, discontinue at least 7 days before surgery
Do not stop prematurely - increases stent thrombosis, MI, and death risk
moa: Prasugrel is a prodrug rapidly hydrolyzed to a thiolactone and then converted (chiefly by CYP3A4 and CYP2B6, with lesser CYP2C9/CYP2C19) to an active metabolite that irreversibly binds the platelet P2Y12 class of ADP receptors. This blocks ADP-mediated activation of the GPIIb/IIIa complex and inhibits platelet aggregation for the lifespan of the platelet.

absolute: Active pathological bleeding (e.g. peptic ulcer or intracranial hemorrhage)
History of prior transient ischemic attack (TIA) or stroke
Hypersensitivity (e.g. anaphylaxis) to prasugrel or any component
relative: Age >=75 years (generally not recommended except high-risk diabetes or prior MI)
Likely to undergo urgent CABG or other surgery
Concomitant warfarin, heparin, fibrinolytics, or chronic NSAIDs
monitor: Signs and symptoms of bleeding (especially if hypotensive after angiography/PCI/CABG)
Platelet count and smear if TTP suspected

preg: There are no human data with prasugrel in pregnancy to inform a drug-associated risk; animal studies showed no structural malformations but a slight decrease in fetal weight at high exposures. Because of the mechanism of action and the identified risk of bleeding (see BOXED WARNING), weigh the benefits and risks, including possible fetal risk, when prescribing to a pregnant woman.
lact: There is no information on the presence of prasugrel in human milk, effects on the breastfed infant, or effects on milk production; metabolites were found in rat milk. Weigh the developmental and health benefits of breastfeeding against the mother's clinical need and any potential adverse effects on the infant.
renal: No dosage adjustment is necessary, including in patients with end-stage renal disease. The active metabolite is not likely to be removed by dialysis.
hepatic: No dosage adjustment is needed in mild to moderate hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh A and B). Prasugrel has not been studied in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C), which may carry an inherent bleeding risk - avoid use.

moderate: Heparin / fibrinolytic therapy - additive bleeding risk
Opioids (e.g. morphine) - delayed and reduced absorption of active metabolite; consider a parenteral antiplatelet agent
minor: CYP3A inducers/inhibitors - prasugrel may be given concomitantly (limited clinical effect)
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; a high-fat meal lowers Cmax and delays Tmax but does not affect AUC
interactions.alcohol: No specific interaction; excess alcohol increases bleeding/GI risk
interactions.diagnostics: May be co-administered with PPIs, H2 blockers, statins, digoxin, heparin, and GPIIb/IIIa inhibitors without dose adjustment

common: Bleeding (the most commonly reported reaction; epistaxis, hematoma, GI bleeding, hematuria)
Hypertension, hypercholesterolemia/hyperlipidemia, headache, back pain, dyspnea, nausea, dizziness (reported in trials)
serious: Major and life-threatening or fatal bleeding (including CABG-related and intracranial)
rare: Angioedema, including in patients with prior thienopyridine hypersensitivity
emergency: TTP (thrombocytopenia, hemolytic anemia, neurologic signs, renal dysfunction, fever)

monitoring: Signs and symptoms of bleeding (suspect bleeding in any hypotensive patient after angiography/PCI/CABG)
Platelet count and peripheral smear if TTP suspected
Adherence - premature discontinuation raises stent thrombosis, MI, and death risk
counsel: Take exactly as prescribed with daily aspirin; do not stop without consulting your cardiologist
This drug can cause serious or fatal bleeding - report unusual bleeding, bruising, blood in urine/stool, or black tarry stools
Tell all doctors and dentists you take prasugrel; it is usually stopped at least 7 days before surgery
Seek urgent care for severe or persistent bleeding or a severe headache
Seek urgent care for signs of TTP (fever, weakness, confusion, easy bruising)
It may take longer than usual to stop bleeding from cuts
pk: About 90% of patients achieve >=50% platelet inhibition by 1 hour after the 60 mg load
Active-metabolite Cmax about 30 minutes after dosing; maximum inhibition ~80%
Active metabolite elimination half-life about 7 hours (range 2-15 h)
Irreversible; platelet aggregation returns to baseline over 5-9 days after stopping
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F); keep in original container; do not break tablet
pearls: BOXED WARNING: significant, sometimes fatal bleeding - contraindicated in active bleeding and in prior TIA/stroke
Generally not recommended at age >=75 except high-risk (diabetes or prior MI) due to fatal/intracranial bleeding risk
Consider 5 mg maintenance if body weight <60 kg
Do not start if urgent CABG likely; discontinue at least 7 days before surgery
Showed greater MI reduction than clopidogrel in TRITON-TIMI 38, but more bleeding
Effect is irreversible - manage major bleeding with platelet transfusion (not dialyzable)
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember on the same day. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and take the next one at the usual time. Do not take two doses at once.
overdose: Platelet inhibition is rapid and irreversible, lasting the life of the platelet, so effect is unlikely to increase further in overdose. Manage bleeding supportively; platelet transfusion may restore clotting ability. The active metabolite is not likely to be removed by dialysis.
